elements.element: Customer has no minimum purchase commitment.
elements.evidence: The clause permits a minimum purchase obligation when expressly stated in a signed Order Form.

elements.element: Customer pays fees only for actual usage or ordered Services.
elements.evidence: The clause allows a commitment and requires a shortfall true-up, so Customer may owe fees for Services not actually used or ordered.

elements.element: Any purchase commitment is limited to the then-current 12-month term.
elements.evidence: The clause states that any commitment applies only to the then-current twelve-month term.

elements.element: Customer may reduce the purchase commitment on 30 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly permits Customer to reduce the commitment on thirty days' written notice.

elements.element: Any commitment shortfall is resolved through a true-up rather than a penalty.
elements.evidence: The clause states that any shortfall is settled by a true-up at the applicable unit price rather than a penalty.

result.reason: The redline fully satisfies the fallback but not the preferred position because signed Order Forms may still impose minimum commitments and associated shortfall payments. It is not minimal because it additionally provides that commitments terminate upon termination of the applicable Order Form, a protection not required to satisfy the fallback. The operative language otherwise removes the original three-year, non-reducible take-or-pay structure without disturbing unrelated terms. Drafting quality is reduced by the cumbersome final compound sentence and the potentially ambiguous relationship between the then-current twelve-month term and termination of the applicable Order Form.
